Chapter overview

Self-Respect Movement traces the movement from Periyar’s Congress exit and its 1925 launch through print, conferences, marriage reform, women’s participation, socialism, overseas networks, Justice Party cooperation and the transition to Dravidar Kazhagam.

Origins & organisationPrint & conferencesMarriage & anti-caste practiceWomen, socialism & diasporaJustice, DK & legacy
Scope, Meaning and Historical Position

The Self-Respect Movement or Suyamariyathai sought social dignity independent of caste, religion, gender, birth and priestly approval, and functioned mainly as a social movement rather than an electoral party.

Meaning of Self-Respect

The Tamil expression for Self-Respect is:

  • Suyamariyathai
  • Suya Mariyathai

The movement maintained that every human being must possess dignity independent of:

  • Caste
  • Religion
  • Birth
  • Gender
  • Wealth
  • Hereditary occupation
  • Priestly approval

The Self-Respect Movement was not merely a campaign for individual confidence. It sought to reconstruct society by removing institutions that treated some people as naturally superior and others as naturally inferior.

Historical Position

The movement was launched in the Madras Presidency in 1925 under the leadership of E. V. Ramasamy, later widely known as Periyar.

It developed between several major political traditions:

  • Nineteenth-century anti-caste reform
  • Non-Brahmin political organisation
  • Justice Party politics
  • Rationalist thought
  • Women’s emancipation
  • Labour and socialist politics
  • Anti-Hindi mobilisation
  • Later Dravidian politics
Nature of the Movement

The movement functioned through:

  • Newspapers
  • Public meetings
  • Conferences
  • District associations
  • Propaganda tours
  • Reform marriages
  • Inter-dining
  • Women’s conferences
  • Anti-caste campaigns
  • Social boycott of discriminatory customs
  • Political alliances

It was primarily a social movement rather than an electoral political party.

Periyar repeatedly described it as a movement intended to restore human dignity and free people intellectually from inherited authority.

Background: Congress, Caste and Communal Representation

Periyar’s experience in the Congress, the Cheranmadevi Gurukulam controversy, Vaikom and the rejection of communal representation formed the immediate background to the movement.

Unequal Social Structure

Early twentieth-century Tamil society was marked by inequalities concerning:

  • Education
  • Government employment
  • Temple access
  • Public roads
  • Drinking water
  • Marriage
  • Religious status
  • Representation in political organisations

Caste influenced both social dignity and access to modern opportunities.

Congress and Communal Representation

Periyar joined the Indian National Congress and participated in:

  • Non-Cooperation
  • Khadi promotion
  • Temperance
  • Anti-untouchability campaigns
  • Provincial Congress organisation

He repeatedly demanded communal representation for non-Brahmin and disadvantaged communities in:

  • Public employment
  • Education
  • Representative institutions

He believed that political independence without social safeguards could transfer authority from British officials to a narrow Indian elite.

Cheranmadevi Gurukulam Controversy

The Cheranmadevi Gurukulam was run by:

  • V. V. S. Aiyar
  • With financial support from Congress leaders and donors

Complaints arose that Brahmin and non-Brahmin students were treated differently, particularly in dining arrangements.

Periyar opposed the discrimination and questioned why an institution receiving public and Congress support should practise caste separation.

The controversy increased his dissatisfaction with the Congress approach to caste.

Vaikom Satyagraha

During 1924–1925, Periyar participated prominently in the Vaikom Satyagraha in Travancore.

The agitation challenged restrictions preventing oppressed communities from using roads around the Vaikom temple.

Vaikom strengthened his conviction that:

  • Caste operated through everyday public restrictions.
  • Religious authority protected social inequality.
  • Social equality required organised confrontation.
Kanchipuram Congress Conference

At the Tamil Nadu Congress conference held at Kanchipuram in November 1925, Periyar’s proposal supporting communal representation was not accepted.

He walked out of the conference and left the Congress.

The Gurukulam controversy, Vaikom experience and rejection of communal representation together formed the immediate background to the Self-Respect Movement.

Periyar’s Exit from Congress and Launch of the Movement

Periyar left the Congress in 1925 and distinguished political freedom from the deeper social freedom required to remove caste, patriarchy and religious domination.

Departure from Congress

Periyar left the Congress in 1925.

He concluded that the national movement was giving greater priority to:

  • Political freedom
  • National unity
  • Restoration of traditional institutions

than to:

  • Caste abolition
  • Communal representation
  • Women’s equality
  • Social dignity

He argued that independence would be incomplete if oppressed people continued to live without self-respect.

Launch of the Movement

The Self-Respect Movement emerged in 1925 after his departure from the Congress.

Periyar became its principal:

  • Leader
  • Organiser
  • Speaker
  • Journalist
  • Ideological propagandist

Associates such as S. Ramanathan and other non-Brahmin activists helped develop its early organisational network.

Political Freedom and Social Freedom

The movement distinguished between:

Political Freedom
  • Removal of British rule
  • Transfer of state power
  • National self-government
Social Freedom
  • Removal of caste hierarchy
  • Gender equality
  • Freedom from religious domination
  • Access to education
  • Equal civil rights
  • Freedom to choose one’s marriage and occupation

The movement argued that political independence without social freedom would preserve internal forms of slavery.

Initial Objectives

The early movement sought to:

  • Create self-respect among oppressed communities
  • Oppose birth-based superiority
  • Remove untouchability
  • Promote communal representation
  • Encourage women’s emancipation
  • Replace religious authority with reason
  • Develop non-Brahmin political and social consciousness

The detailed philosophical principles are reserved for Chapter 26.

Early Organisers, Self-Respect Leagues and District Expansion

Local leagues, reading rooms, volunteers, women’s groups and district conferences converted the movement from a leadership initiative into a wider organisational network.

Organisational Growth

The movement did not initially possess a rigid central party structure.

It expanded through:

  • Local Self-Respect associations
  • District conferences
  • Reading rooms
  • Youth organisations
  • Volunteers
  • Women’s groups
  • Newspaper agents
  • Public speakers

By the end of 1926, Self-Respect leagues and propaganda networks had appeared in several parts of the Tamil districts.

Important Early Organisers

Important personalities included:

  • S. Ramanathan
  • W. P. A. Soundarapandian
  • Kuthoosi Gurusamy
  • Sami Chidambaranar
  • Pattukkottai Alagirisamy
  • A. Ponnambalanar
  • K. A. P. Viswanatham
  • S. Gurusamy
  • P. Jeevanandham
  • M. Singaravelar
  • Moovalur Ramamirtham Ammaiyar
  • Nagammal
  • Kannammal
  • Kunjitham Gurusamy

Not every organiser remained in the movement permanently. Some later joined:

  • Socialist organisations
  • Communist organisations
  • Justice Party
  • Dravidar Kazhagam
  • DMK
  • Other reform bodies
District-Level Activity

Local conferences were organised in regions such as:

  • Chengalpattu
  • Erode
  • Tirunelveli
  • Thanjavur
  • Madurai
  • Ramanathapuram
  • Virudhunagar
  • Tiruchirappalli
  • Coimbatore
  • South Arcot

District organisers translated the movement’s broad ideas into practical actions such as:

  • Inter-caste dining
  • Reform marriages
  • Removal of caste suffixes
  • Women’s meetings
  • Public debates
  • Opposition to untouchability
Social Composition

The movement drew support from:

  • Non-Brahmin middle classes
  • Teachers
  • Students
  • Small traders
  • Journalists
  • Women activists
  • Workers
  • Sections of oppressed communities
  • Tamil migrants overseas

Its support was substantial but uneven across regions and communities.

Kudi Arasu, Revolt and the Propaganda Network

Kudi Arasu, Revolt and related journals created an alternative public sphere for anti-caste, rationalist, feminist and social-reform propaganda.

Kudi Arasu

Kudi Arasu means:

  • Republic
  • People’s Rule

Important facts:

  • Began on 2 May 1925
  • Published from Erode
  • Tamil weekly
  • Founded by Periyar
  • Became the principal voice of the Self-Respect Movement

Kudi Arasu published material on:

  • Caste
  • Religion
  • Communal representation
  • Women
  • Marriage
  • Rationalism
  • Labour
  • Politics
  • International movements
Style of Communication

The publication used:

  • Direct Tamil
  • Questions and answers
  • Editorials
  • Reports of reform marriages
  • Conference resolutions
  • Reader letters
  • Translations
  • Satire
  • Political cartoons

This style allowed complex social ideas to reach readers outside universities and professional circles.

Revolt

Important facts:

  • English weekly
  • Began on 7 November 1928
  • Associated with Periyar and the Self-Respect circle
  • Addressed English-educated readers in India and overseas

Revolt discussed:

  • Caste inequality
  • Women’s rights
  • Religion
  • Nationalism
  • Social revolution
  • International politics
Other Publications

Later publications connected with the wider movement included:

  • Puratchi — 1933
  • Pagutharivu — 1934
  • Viduthalai — from 1935
  • Samadharmam
  • Puduvai Murasu
  • Other district journals

Detailed rationalist publication history belongs to Chapter 23.

Colonial Repression

Movement publications faced:

  • Security demands
  • Confiscation
  • Sedition proceedings
  • Bans
  • Prosecution of editors and publishers

When one publication was restricted, activists often started another.

Importance

The newspaper network:

  • Connected local branches
  • Recorded movement activities
  • Publicised new social practices
  • Trained writers and speakers
  • Reached the Tamil diaspora
  • Created an alternative public sphere

The movement’s growth cannot be understood without Kudi Arasu.

First Provincial Self-Respect Conference at Chengalpattu

The Chengalpattu conference of 1929 gave the movement a province-wide programme covering caste, women, education, property, employment and social equality.

Conference Details

The First Madras Provincial Self-Respect Conference was held at:

  • Chengalpattu
  • 17–18 February 1929

It was presided over by:

  • W. P. A. Soundarapandian

Prominent participants included:

  • Periyar
  • Kuthoosi Gurusamy
  • Moovalur Ramamirtham Ammaiyar
  • Justice Party leaders
  • District-level Self-Respect organisers
Importance

The conference transformed a growing propaganda movement into a clearly visible province-wide organisation.

It:

  • Defined the movement’s public programme
  • Brought activists from different districts together
  • Passed resolutions on social reform
  • Created a common campaign framework
  • Attracted major public and press attention
Major Areas of Resolution

The resolutions addressed:

  • Caste distinctions
  • Untouchability
  • Caste suffixes
  • Caste and religious marks
  • Priest-controlled ceremonies
  • Inter-caste dining
  • Communal representation
  • Women’s education
  • Women’s employment
  • Women’s property rights
  • Widow remarriage
  • Marriage expenses
  • Compulsory elementary education

These resolutions are introduced here as conference decisions. Their detailed ideological basis belongs to Chapter 26.

Women’s Rights

The conference demanded that women should receive:

  • Education
  • Employment based on qualification
  • Rights in family property
  • Freedom in marriage
  • Protection from oppressive customs

These demands were radical because women’s legal and property rights were still severely limited.

Economic Dimension

The conference also connected social equality with freedom from economic exploitation.

Self-respect was therefore not defined only as the removal of ritual humiliation.

It included access to:

  • Education
  • Employment
  • Property
  • Public power

The Chengalpattu conference became the movement’s most important foundational conference.

Volunteers’ Conference and the First Recorded Self-Respect Marriage

Volunteers translated movement ideas into daily practice, while the Gurusamy–Kunjitham marriage became a documented model of the Self-Respect marriage form.

Self-Respect Volunteers

The movement depended on volunteers to:

  • Organise meetings
  • Distribute publications
  • Conduct processions
  • Protect speakers
  • Arrange reform marriages
  • Visit villages
  • Oppose caste discrimination
  • Collect subscriptions
Pattukkottai Volunteers’ Conference

The first important Self-Respect Volunteers’ Conference was held at:

  • Pattukkottai
  • 25 May 1929

It was presided over by:

  • Kuthoosi Gurusamy

The volunteers were expected to practise movement reforms in their personal lives rather than merely support them in speeches.

Self-Respect Marriage

Self-Respect marriages rejected the compulsory authority of:

  • Brahmin priests
  • Sanskrit mantras
  • Sacred fire
  • Expensive religious rituals
  • Horoscope matching
  • Caste approval

The marriage was based on:

  • Consent
  • Public declaration
  • Mutual acceptance
  • Presence of witnesses
  • Simple ceremony

Detailed principles belong to Chapter 26.

Kuthoosi Gurusamy and Kunjitham

The marriage between:

  • Kuthoosi Gurusamy
  • Kunjitham

was conducted on:

  • 8 December 1929

It was presided over by Periyar.

It is widely described as the first recorded Self-Respect marriage conducted completely without Hindu ritual.

Historical Caution

Reform marriages and inter-caste marriages had occurred before 1929.

The Gurusamy–Kunjitham marriage is important because it became a publicly recorded model specifically identified with the Self-Respect Movement.

Social Significance

Such marriages challenged:

  • Caste endogamy
  • Priestly monopoly
  • Excessive expenditure
  • Horoscope-based decision-making
  • Family control over adult consent

They converted the movement’s social criticism into an alternative institution.

Erode and Virudhunagar Provincial Conferences

The Erode and Virudhunagar conferences expanded the movement’s provincial organisation and linked social reform with economic and educational questions.

Second Provincial Conference

The Second Provincial Self-Respect Conference was held at:

  • Erode
  • May 1930

It was presided over by:

  • M. R. Jayakar

The conference expanded discussion beyond ritual reform to include:

  • Social equality
  • Economic inequality
  • Education
  • Public employment
  • Temple resources
  • Women’s rights
  • Rationalist propaganda

The associated gatherings included conferences and meetings for:

  • Women
  • Youth
  • Volunteers
  • Reform workers
Erode as a Movement Centre

Erode became important because it was:

  • Periyar’s home region
  • Publication centre of Kudi Arasu
  • Meeting point for movement organisers
  • Later centre of the Erode socialist discussions
Third Provincial Conference

The Third Provincial Self-Respect Conference was held at:

  • Virudhunagar
  • August 1931

Sources commonly identify:

  • R. K. Shanmukham Chetty

as its presiding figure.

The conference continued demands for:

  • Caste abolition
  • Wider education
  • Women’s emancipation
  • Representation for disadvantaged communities
  • Simplification of ceremonies
  • Rationalist social reform
Conference Sequence

The three principal provincial conferences were:

1. Chengalpattu — 1929 2. Erode — 1930 3. Virudhunagar — 1931

Together they:

  • Defined the movement’s organisational programme
  • Created district networks
  • Trained speakers
  • Standardised reform practices
  • Expanded the role of women and volunteers
Historical Caution

The movement also conducted many:

  • District conferences
  • Volunteer conferences
  • Women’s conferences
  • Youth meetings

These should not be confused with the three main provincial conferences.

Women Leaders and Women’s Participation

Women participated as organisers, writers, speakers, protesters and reformers, not merely as beneficiaries of a male-led campaign.

Importance of Women

Women were not merely beneficiaries of the Self-Respect Movement.

They participated as:

  • Organisers
  • Speakers
  • Editors
  • Writers
  • Conference delegates
  • Protesters
  • Marriage reformers
  • Anti-Hindi activists
  • Prisoners
  • Fundraisers
Nagammal

Nagammal was Periyar’s wife and an important public activist.

She participated in:

  • Temperance campaigns
  • Vaikom-related mobilisation
  • Self-Respect propaganda
  • Overseas movement tours
  • Publication and organisational work

She helped maintain movement activity during periods when Periyar faced arrest or travel.

Kannammal

Kannammal, Periyar’s sister, participated in:

  • Movement publications
  • Women’s organisation
  • Public propaganda
  • Anti-caste and rationalist activity
Moovalur Ramamirtham Ammaiyar

Moovalur Ramamirtham became an important campaigner against:

  • Devadasi exploitation
  • Patriarchy
  • Religious control of women
  • Child marriage
  • Denial of women’s education

She spoke at Self-Respect conferences and used writing and public organisation to mobilise women.

Kunjitham Gurusamy

Kunjitham:

  • Was a teacher and activist
  • Wrote on women’s rights
  • Participated in movement conferences
  • Entered a Self-Respect marriage with Kuthoosi Gurusamy

Her public marriage demonstrated the participation of women as active decision-makers rather than passive subjects of reform.

S. Dharmambal

S. Dharmambal worked for:

  • Women’s education
  • Widow remarriage
  • Tamil education
  • Devadasi abolition
  • Anti-Hindi mobilisation

She helped organise the Tamil Nadu Women’s Conference of 1938.

Title “Periyar”

At the Tamil Nadu Women’s Conference held in Madras on:

  • 13 November 1938

women activists conferred the title:

  • Periyar
  • Meaning respected elder or great person

on E. V. Ramasamy.

Other Women

Other participants included:

  • Neelambigai Ammaiyar
  • Indirani Balasubramaniam
  • Narayani Ammal
  • Ramamirtham’s fellow organisers
  • District-level women whose names appeared in conference and arrest records
Historical Importance

The movement gave women space to speak publicly about:

  • Marriage
  • Sexual morality
  • Property
  • Divorce
  • Widowhood
  • Education
  • Reproductive freedom

However, women still worked within organisations whose principal leadership was predominantly male.

Anti-Caste Campaigns and Social Practices

Anti-caste practice included removing caste suffixes, inter-dining, inter-caste marriage, common access and rejection of priestly and ritual hierarchy.

From Resolution to Practice

The movement attempted to convert conference resolutions into changes in everyday behaviour.

Important practices included:

  • Removal of caste suffixes
  • Rejection of caste titles
  • Inter-caste dining
  • Inter-caste marriage
  • Widow remarriage
  • Admission of all communities to common events
  • Refusal to employ priests
  • Use of Tamil instead of Sanskrit in ceremonies
  • Opposition to separate seating and dining
  • Promotion of education for oppressed communities
Caste Names

Activists were encouraged to remove caste suffixes from personal names.

The purpose was to prevent a person’s caste from determining:

  • Honour
  • Occupation
  • Marriage opportunity
  • Public treatment
  • Political status
Caste Marks

Conferences questioned the public use of caste-specific marks and clothing when they operated as symbols of superiority and inferiority.

Inter-Dining

Common dining was organised at:

  • Conferences
  • Reform meetings
  • Marriages
  • Volunteer camps

It directly challenged restrictions on:

  • Touch
  • Food sharing
  • Seating
  • Water
  • Common kitchens
Inter-Caste Marriage

The movement encouraged marriages across:

  • Castes
  • Sub-castes
  • Social divisions

Marriage was considered central because caste reproduces itself through strict endogamy.

Public Access

Movement supporters campaigned against denial of:

  • Roads
  • Schools
  • Wells
  • Public halls
  • Lodging
  • Government institutions
Relationship with Adi Dravida Politics

The movement opposed untouchability and supported safeguards for oppressed communities.

It also supported B. R. Ambedkar’s right to represent the Depressed Classes during major constitutional debates.

However, relations between intermediate non-Brahmin communities and Adi Dravidas remained uneven.

The movement’s rejection of Brahminical hierarchy did not automatically eliminate caste discrimination among all non-Brahmin groups.

Self-Respect Marriages and Their Legal Recognition

Self-Respect marriages replaced compulsory priestly ritual with consent and public declaration and later gained statutory recognition through Tamil Nadu’s Section 7-A amendment.

Purpose of the Marriage Reform

Self-Respect marriages aimed to make marriage:

  • Simple
  • Inexpensive
  • Based on consent
  • Free from hereditary priesthood
  • Open to inter-caste couples
  • Compatible with widow remarriage
  • Independent of Sanskrit ritual

The movement opposed the idea that a marriage became valid only through a priest or sacred ceremony.

Common Forms

A Self-Respect marriage could involve:

  • Declaration of mutual acceptance
  • Exchange of garlands
  • Exchange of rings
  • Signing a written agreement
  • Presence of relatives or friends
  • A speech explaining equality and responsibility

The tying of a thali could be included or omitted according to the couple’s choice.

Social Problems Faced

Before legal recognition, couples faced difficulties concerning:

  • Validity of marriage
  • Legitimacy of children
  • Inheritance
  • Property rights
  • Registration
  • Recognition by public authorities

Despite these risks, many couples used the ceremony as an act of social reform.

Legal Recognition

After the DMK came to power under C. N. Annadurai, Tamil Nadu amended the Hindu Marriage Act.

Section 7-A legally recognised:

  • Suyamariyathai marriages
  • Seerthiruththa marriages
  • Other marriages conducted through equivalent forms of mutual declaration

The Tamil Nadu amendment was enacted in 1967.

The provision recognises a marriage solemnised in the presence of relatives, friends or other persons through:

  • Mutual declaration
  • Exchange of garlands or rings
  • Tying of the thali

These are alternatives; every form is not compulsory.

Historical Importance

The law:

  • Gave legal security to an institution created by a social movement
  • Reduced priestly control over marriage
  • Recognised simple ceremonies
  • Protected couples who chose reformist marriage forms

Detailed marriage principles belong to Chapter 26, while Anna’s legislative role belongs to Chapter 29.

Socialism, Singaravelar and the Erode Programme

The Erode Programme attempted to connect caste and gender reform with socialism, labour rights and economic equality without converting the movement into a communist party.

International Context

The Great Depression and the spread of socialist ideas influenced political movements throughout the world.

Self-Respect activists began to ask whether social equality was possible without addressing:

  • Land ownership
  • Labour exploitation
  • Poverty
  • Unequal wages
  • Concentration of wealth
Periyar’s Overseas Tour

Between 1931 and 1932, Periyar travelled through several countries, including the Soviet Union and parts of Europe.

He observed:

  • Public education
  • Social organisation
  • Labour politics
  • State institutions
  • Socialist economic experiments

He returned to India in November 1932.

Singaravelar

M. Singaravelar brought to the movement:

  • Labour organisation
  • Socialist thought
  • Materialism
  • Scientific education
  • Communist literature

He argued that caste oppression and economic exploitation should be opposed together.

Erode Programme

A meeting was held at Periyar’s residence in Erode on:

  • 28–29 December 1932

The discussions involved Periyar, Singaravelar and Self-Respect activists.

The resulting programme is commonly called:

  • Erode Plan
  • Erode Programme

It sought to link:

  • Self-Respect social reform
  • Economic equality
  • Labour rights
  • Socialist propaganda
  • Reduction of economic exploitation
Publications and Translation

The movement circulated or discussed writings associated with:

  • Karl Marx
  • Friedrich Engels
  • Socialist movements
  • Bertrand Russell
  • Robert Ingersoll
  • Charles Bradlaugh
  • Bhagat Singh

P. Jeevanandham translated Bhagat Singh’s Why I Am an Atheist into Tamil.

Internal Differences

The socialist phase produced disagreement over whether the movement should concentrate on:

  • Social reform
  • Class struggle
  • Electoral politics
  • Justice Party cooperation
  • Anti-colonial nationalism

Some activists, including Jeevanandham, later moved towards socialist and communist organisations.

The Self-Respect Movement did not become a unified communist party.

Overseas Spread in Malaya, Singapore and Sri Lanka

Print, migration and Periyar’s tour spread Self-Respect ideas through Malaya, Singapore, Ceylon and other overseas Tamil communities.

Tamil Migration

Large Tamil communities lived in:

  • British Malaya
  • Singapore
  • Ceylon
  • Burma

They included:

  • Plantation workers
  • Labourers
  • Traders
  • Teachers
  • Journalists
  • Clerks
  • Religious leaders

Overseas Tamil society also reproduced divisions involving:

  • Caste
  • Religion
  • Language
  • Social status
Periyar’s Malaya Tour

Periyar travelled to British Malaya from:

  • December 1929 to January 1930

He was accompanied by movement associates, including Nagammal.

He participated in meetings in places such as:

  • Penang
  • Ipoh
  • Kuala Lumpur
  • Singapore

At Ipoh, he addressed a Tamil reform gathering.

Overseas Organisations

Self-Respect ideas influenced organisations such as:

  • Tamil Reform Association
  • Reading circles
  • Tamil newspapers
  • Social-reform societies
  • Youth organisations

Important overseas activists included:

  • G. Sarangapani
  • Tamil journalists and reform organisers
  • Estate-level speakers and volunteers
Main Overseas Issues

Overseas Self-Respect discussion addressed:

  • Caste discrimination
  • Temple administration
  • Marriage reform
  • Tamil education
  • Labour conditions
  • Representation of Indians
  • Migrant identity
  • Relations with Malayan society
Transformation in Malaya

The movement was not copied without change.

Malayan Tamil activists adapted it to local concerns involving:

  • Migrant citizenship
  • Labour
  • Education
  • Indian representation
  • Tamil identity
  • Multi-ethnic politics
Historical Importance

The overseas network demonstrates that the Self-Respect Movement was:

  • Transregional
  • Print-based
  • Connected to migration
  • Influential beyond the territorial boundaries of Tamil Nadu

Its diaspora influence was particularly strong during the interwar years.

Justice Party Cooperation and Anti-Hindi Agitation

Justice Party cooperation and the anti-Hindi agitation brought the social movement into closer organisational contact with provincial non-Brahmin politics.

Initial Difference

The Justice Party and Self-Respect Movement were not originally identical.

Justice Party
  • Electoral political party
  • Formed ministries
  • Worked through legislatures
  • Prioritised representation and public employment
Self-Respect Movement
  • Social movement
  • Used propaganda and reform campaigns
  • Questioned caste, religion, marriage and patriarchy
  • Initially remained outside formal electoral politics
Growing Cooperation

During the late 1920s and 1930s:

  • Justice Party leaders attended Self-Respect conferences.
  • Self-Respect activists supported communal representation.
  • Both opposed Congress dominance.
  • The movement’s radical social programme influenced younger Justice supporters.

The Erode Programme was considered for inclusion in broader Justice Party politics, although cooperation was never free from disagreement.

Election of 1937

The Justice Party suffered a major defeat in the 1937 provincial election.

The Congress formed the government under:

  • C. Rajagopalachari

The introduction of compulsory Hindi in selected schools produced a new common campaign.

Anti-Hindi Agitation

The agitation of 1937–1940 was supported by:

  • Self-Respect Movement
  • Justice Party
  • Tamil scholars
  • Women’s organisations
  • Students
  • Muslim Tamil organisations
  • Other language activists

Methods included:

  • Public meetings
  • School picketing
  • Processions
  • Black-flag protests
  • Anti-Hindi days
  • Arrest campaigns
  • Women’s mobilisation
Women’s Conference of 1938

The Tamil Nadu Women’s Conference of 13 November 1938:

  • Supported the anti-Hindi campaign
  • Demonstrated women’s organisational role
  • Conferred the title Periyar on E. V. Ramasamy
Periyar and Justice Party Leadership

Periyar was chosen to lead the Justice Party in late 1938 while he was associated with the anti-Hindi agitation and imprisonment.

The two movements increasingly shared:

  • Organisation
  • Publications
  • Leaders
  • Social programme

Detailed Justice Party history belongs to Chapter 22, and detailed anti-Hindi history to Chapter 21.

Transition from Self-Respect Movement to Dravidar Kazhagam

In 1944 the Justice Party, not the Self-Respect Movement itself, was transformed into Dravidar Kazhagam under a programme strongly shaped by Self-Respect ideas.

Ideological Convergence

By the late 1930s, the Justice Party’s political organisation and the Self-Respect Movement’s social programme had moved closer.

The combined current emphasised:

  • Communal representation
  • Caste abolition
  • Rationalism
  • Women’s equality
  • Anti-Hindi mobilisation
  • Dravidian identity
  • Opposition to hereditary privilege
Periyar’s Leadership

Periyar’s leadership changed the Justice Party’s orientation.

The organisation increasingly moved away from:

  • Elite constitutional politics
  • British titles
  • Government nominations
  • Electoral office seeking

and towards:

  • Mass social propaganda
  • Rationalism
  • Anti-caste agitation
  • Non-electoral organisation
Salem Conference

At the Salem conference held on:

  • 27 August 1944

the Justice Party was transformed into:

  • Dravidar Kazhagam
  • DK

Major organisational decisions included:

  • Renunciation of British titles
  • Giving up nominated offices
  • Removal of caste suffixes
  • Withdrawal from electoral politics
  • Priority to social transformation
Position of the Self-Respect Movement

The Self-Respect Movement did not disappear as an idea.

Its methods and principles became central to:

  • Dravidar Kazhagam
  • Later Dravidian organisations
  • Marriage reform
  • Rationalist campaigns
  • Social-justice politics
Chapter Boundary

This topic provides only the transition.

Detailed coverage belongs to:

  • Chapter 25 — Dravidian Movement
  • Chapter 27 — Principles of the Dravidian Movement
  • Chapter 28 — Contributions of Periyar
  • Chapter 29 — Contributions of Anna

Periyar did not transform the Self-Respect Movement into an ordinary electoral party. He transformed the Justice Party into a non-electoral social organisation shaped strongly by Self-Respect principles.

Achievements, Criticisms and Historical Impact

The movement reshaped public debate on caste, marriage, women, language and rationalism while facing limitations involving caste persistence, economic organisation and centralised leadership.

Major Achievements
Social Dignity

The movement made self-respect and human dignity central political ideas.

It encouraged people to reject:

  • Caste humiliation
  • Hereditary inferiority
  • Priestly domination
  • Unequal marriage customs
Marriage Reform

It created a practical alternative to expensive and priest-controlled marriage ceremonies.

Its marriage system later gained legal recognition.

Women’s Participation

The movement created spaces for women to discuss:

  • Property
  • Education
  • Employment
  • Marriage
  • Divorce
  • Widowhood
  • Reproductive freedom
Rationalist Public Sphere

It encouraged people to:

  • Question authority
  • Debate religion
  • Examine superstition
  • Read scientific and political literature
  • Judge customs by their effects on human welfare
Public Language

The use of accessible Tamil enabled social-reform ideas to reach:

  • Villages
  • Small towns
  • Workers
  • Women
  • Young people
  • Overseas Tamils
Influence on Public Policy

Its long-term influence can be seen in debates concerning:

  • Reservation
  • Communal representation
  • Women’s rights
  • Self-Respect marriage
  • Caste names
  • Language policy
  • Social welfare
  • Temple administration
Criticisms and Limitations
Uneven Caste Transformation

The movement criticised Brahminical hierarchy but could not eliminate caste discrimination among non-Brahmin communities.

Intermediate-caste dominance remained a serious problem.

Relationship with Adi Dravida Movements

The movement supported anti-untouchability and political safeguards, but Adi Dravida leaders maintained independent organisations because their needs were not always fully represented by broader non-Brahmin politics.

Confrontational Methods

Its:

  • Anti-religious rhetoric
  • Iconoclasm
  • Burning of texts or symbols
  • Satirical attacks

alienated many religious believers.

Supporters regarded these methods as necessary to destroy fear; critics regarded them as offensive and polarising.

Limited Economic Organisation

Although the Erode Programme addressed economic equality, the movement’s strongest and most durable work remained in:

  • Social reform
  • Cultural politics
  • Marriage
  • Caste
  • Language

It did not build a unified long-term labour or peasant organisation.

Leadership Structure

The movement enabled many women and local activists to participate, but its principal public leadership remained heavily centred on Periyar.

Balanced Assessment

The Self-Respect Movement did not abolish caste or patriarchy.

Its major achievement was changing the terms of public debate.

Practices once accepted as sacred or unchangeable became open to:

  • Criticism
  • Reform
  • Legal regulation
  • Personal rejection

The movement became one of the principal foundations of modern Tamil Nadu’s social-justice and Dravidian political traditions.

Rapid Revision and High-Yield Distinctions

The final topic consolidates the movement’s chronology, leaders, publications, conferences, institutional transitions and common TNPSC examination distinctions.

  • 1925 — Cheranmadevi Gurukulam controversy intensified
  • November 1925 — Periyar left Congress at Kanchipuram
  • 1925 — Self-Respect Movement launched
  • 2 May 1925 — Kudi Arasu began
  • 1926 — Self-Respect leagues expanded in Tamil districts
  • 7 November 1928 — Revolt began

  • 25 May 1929 — Self-Respect Volunteers’ Conference at Pattukkottai
  • 8 December 1929 — Recorded Self-Respect marriage of Kuthoosi Gurusamy and Kunjitham
  • December 1929–January 1930 — Periyar’s Malaya tour

High-Yield Distinctions
Self-Respect Movement versus Justice Party

Self-Respect Movement

  • Social movement
  • Began in 1925
  • Caste, marriage, women and rationalism
  • Did not initially contest elections

Justice Party

  • Political party
  • Formed in 1916
  • Contested elections
  • Formed provincial ministries
Self-Respect Movement versus Dravidar Kazhagam

Self-Respect Movement

  • Began in 1925
  • Broad social-reform movement
  • Operated through conferences and propaganda

Dravidar Kazhagam

  • Emerged in 1944
  • Organisational successor to Justice Party
  • Incorporated Self-Respect principles
  • Non-electoral organisation
Self-Respect Movement versus Rationalist Movement

Self-Respect Movement

  • Organised social campaign
  • Marriage, caste, women and dignity

Rationalist Movement

  • Wider intellectual method
  • Reason, evidence and criticism of authority

Rationalism was a central component of Self-Respect but was not identical to it.

Political Freedom versus Social Freedom

Political freedom

  • End of colonial rule

Social freedom

  • End of caste, gender and religious oppression

The movement argued that one without the other was incomplete.

Chengalpattu versus Erode Conference

Chengalpattu

  • 1929
  • First provincial conference
  • W. P. A. Soundarapandian
  • Foundational resolutions

Erode

  • 1930
  • Second provincial conference
  • M. R. Jayakar
  • Expanded social and economic programme
Provincial Conference versus Volunteers’ Conference

Provincial conference

  • General movement programme
  • Leaders and district delegates

Volunteers’ conference

  • Training and organisation of field workers
  • Pattukkottai, 1929
Reform Marriage versus Self-Respect Marriage

Reform marriage

  • General category of simplified or socially progressive marriage

Self-Respect marriage

  • Specifically associated with Suyamariyathai principles
  • Mutual consent
  • No compulsory priest or ritual
  • Later recognised under Section 7-A in Tamil Nadu
Kuthoosi Gurusamy versus S. Gurusamy

Kuthoosi Gurusamy was:

  • A prominent journalist and movement activist
  • President of the Pattukkottai Volunteers’ Conference
  • Husband of Kunjitham in the recorded 1929 Self-Respect marriage

Do not confuse him with other activists who also used the name Gurusamy.

Social Equality versus Economic Equality

Social equality

  • Removal of caste and gender hierarchy

Economic equality

  • Reduction of exploitation and unequal control of wealth

The Erode Programme attempted to connect both.

Periyar’s Congress Exit versus Justice Party Leadership

Congress exit

  • 1925
  • Communal representation and caste disagreements

Justice Party leadership

  • Late 1938
  • More than a decade after the movement began
First Anti-Hindi Agitation versus Self-Respect Movement

Self-Respect Movement

  • Began in 1925
  • Wider social-reform movement

Anti-Hindi agitation

  • Began in 1937
  • One major campaign supported by Self-Respect activists
Exam Traps
  • The Self-Respect Movement was launched in 1925.
  • Kudi Arasu also began in 1925.
  • The Self-Respect Movement and Justice Party were not originally the same organisation.
  • Cheranmadevi Gurukulam and communal representation were important reasons for Periyar’s Congress exit.
  • The first provincial conference was held at Chengalpattu in 1929.
  • W. P. A. Soundarapandian presided over the Chengalpattu conference.
  • The Volunteers’ Conference was held at Pattukkottai in 1929.
  • Kuthoosi Gurusamy presided over the Volunteers’ Conference.
  • The Gurusamy–Kunjitham marriage occurred on 8 December 1929.
  • The second provincial conference was held at Erode in 1930.
  • The third provincial conference was held at Virudhunagar in 1931.
  • The Erode Programme belongs to 1932.
  • Singaravelar connected Self-Respect with socialist thought.
  • Women were organisers and speakers, not merely beneficiaries.
  • The title Periyar was conferred at a women’s conference in 1938.
  • Self-Respect marriages existed before they received legal recognition.
  • Tamil Nadu legally recognised Self-Respect marriages through the 1967 amendment.
  • The Self-Respect Movement did not become the DMK directly.
  • Justice Party became Dravidar Kazhagam in 1944.
  • DMK was formed separately in 1949.
  • Detailed Self-Respect principles belong to Chapter 26.
  • Detailed Dravidian Movement history belongs to Chapter 25.
  • Periyar’s complete contribution belongs to Chapter 28.
  • Anna’s complete contribution belongs to Chapter 29.
